catalog_quote: On the basis of new fieldwork data, I arrived at an alternative analysis of the word prosodic system of Ma'ya, with only three tonemes, restricted to the final syllable, and contrastive lexical stress (either penultimate or final). ... Assuming that this analysis is correct, Ma'ya is the only tone language in the world that has been demonstrated to feature lexically contrastive stress. [p.2] ... Ma'ya features three paradigmatically contrastive tones. To begin with, there are the High and the Rising tonemes (/3/ and /12/ respectively). The distribution of these tonemes is limited to the final syllable of content word roots. Paradoxically, lexical stress functions as a third paradigmatically contrastive element, in contrast with the High and Rise tonemes. ... Lexical stress is syntagmatically contrastive in polysyllabic words, either on the penultimate or on the final syllable. [p.53] ..…
sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are Glottolog duplicates of the catalog's own deciding source, Remijsen's 2001 LOT 49 dissertation (Glottolog dates one copy 2002 with a dead Papuaweb URL; the other is the MPI handle copy behind a bot wall). The open LOT PDF is held by the project and was re-read: it confirms the 'lexical' coding (contrastive penult vs final stress, minimal pairs, acoustic support) and the catalog's secondary rule (contrast confined to penult-/a/ words; constraints I-III pp.106-107, 122). Additional stress-relevant works found via Crossref and the Glottolog langdoc list but not in the item list: Remijsen 2002 LabPhon 7 chapter (published version of ch. III; paywalled, medium priority) and Remijsen 2001 Language and Speech (dialectal tone variation; paywalled, low), plus van der Leeden 1983/1993 (print only; earlier four-toneme analysis that Remijsen supersedes), van der Leeden 1997 and Kawira 1986 (not found). Arnold 2018 (held by the project) is a consistent secondary summary. No change to the catalog is warranted; no new statement supersedes the current source.

new_statements.quote: I. If a polysyllabic word has a vowel other than /a/ in the penultimate syllable, it can only have penultimate stress. Alternatively, when a polysyllabic word has the vowel /a/ in the penultimate syllable, then stress is contrastive, either on the penultimate or on the final syllable. II. If a polysyllabic word has a vowel other than /a/ in the penultimate syllable, the vowels of penultimate and final syllables are usually the same. ... III. Words with penultimate stress can only have a High toneme; words with final stress can have either the High or the Rise tonemes. [pp.106-107] ... Contrastive stress, therefore, is limited to words with the penultimate syllable vowel /a/, and mostly with final vowel also being /a/ [p.122]

tone_statements.quote: Remijsen (2001b: 50, 70) analyzes Maˈya as having three tonemes: Rise/Low (/¹²/), Fall (/²¹/), and High (/³/). Tones are restricted to word-final syllables. In addition to tone, Maˈya has contrastive lexical stress (/ˈ/), which is restricted to penultimate and final syllables. ... As an illustration, the minimal triplet ˈsa¹² ‘to sweep’, ˈsa³ ‘to climb’, and ˈsa ‘one’ contains the tonemes Rise, High, and Fall, respectively. Remijsen analyzes ˈsa ‘one’ as underlyingly toneless. All three words are stressed.
tone_statements.summary: 3 tonemes on the word-final syllable plus contrastive stress (penult/final), all data from Remijsen 2001b; Fall = stress with no underlying toneme (table 5.3); Kawe and Wauyai dialects non-tonal.

tone_statements.quote: Following Remijsen (2001a, 2001b, 2002), who builds on a tonal analysis first proposed in van der Leeden (1993), all these varieties are analysed with both lexical tone and lexical stress. Tone specifications in all languages are almost exclusively culminative (i.e., there is a maximum of on tone per word) and restricted to word‑final syllables. In the Maˈya dialects, the contrast is between High, Rise, and toneless syllables [p. 13] ... Stress, on the other hand, falls unpredictably on either the penultimate or final syllable of polysyllabic words in all varieties; in at least Salawati Maˈya, phonetic correlates of stress are increased duration, less centralised vowels, and increased intensity when compared with unstressed syllables (Remijsen 2001a: 54–68). The combination of lexical stress and lexical tone leads to minimal pairs such as Salawati Maˈya ˈmana³ ‘light (of weight)’ vs maˈna³ ‘grease’—both bearing High tone realised on the final syllable, but the former with penultimate stress and the latter with final stress. audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the held Remijsen 2001 LOT dissertation at the stated pages (p.2, p.53; sub-regularities pp.105-106; secondary locators p.18, p.49 also verified). The source is the definitive fieldwork-based phonological and instrumental study of Ma'ya word prosody by the specialist on the language, superseding van der Leeden 1993; no reference grammar has been published, and the later literature (Arnold 2018, downloaded, pp.9-10) restates the same analysis: lexical tone confined to the final syllable, lexical stress contrastive between penult and final. Coding 'lexical', right edge, is exactly what the source says. works still to obtain are low-priority corroboration (refereed versions, the superseded competing analysis), none likely to change the classification.

tone.summary: Tonogenesis of Ma'ya-Matbat tone; Ma'ya H/Rise(/Fall) system as comparandum.
tone.says: Bottom-up comparison of tonal correspondences across Ambel, Ma'ya and Matbat; concluded tone was innovated in a common ancestor of Ma'ya and Matbat and separately in Ambel (per web summary and Arnold 2025 OL sec.1/sec.7, where the author revises that conclusion). Bears on the origin of the Ma'ya (incl. Wauyai) High/Rise system.

To begin with, there are the High and the Rising tonemes (/3/ and /12/ respectively). The distribution of these tonemes is limited to the final syllable of content word roots. Paradoxically, lexical stress functions as a third paradigmatically contrastive element ...

tone.summary: Ma'ya (Salawati data): word-final culminative tone High vs Rise vs toneless + independent lexical stress (penult/final).
tone.says: Reanalyses van der Leeden's four-toneme system as three paradigmatically contrastive values on the final syllable of content roots - High /3/, Rise /12/ and toneless (stress only) - plus lexically contrastive stress on the penult or final syllable, independent of tone; acoustic study shows stress is cued by duration, vowel quality, spectral tilt, not by f0, while tone is cued by f0; Ma'ya + Papiamentu named as the only reported hybrid systems with contrastive stress AND lexical tone.

tone.says: Citation + Remijsen's summary (2001:47-50): descriptive phonology of Salawati Ma'ya distinguishing four tonemes - High /3/, Rising /12/, Falling /21/, Low /1/ - marked on every syllable (e.g. Ga'le12 Ma'ya3), with variable stress and a stress-shift rule and morphological tone; Remijsen calls it 'the discovery of lexical tone in Ma'ya by van der Leeden' and reanalyses it with fewer tonemes.
